media:group.media:title: Water tower demolition
media:group.media:description:
This 124-foot-tall, 300,000-gallon water tank was built for the U.S. Army in 1941, when the Brookhaven Lab site was still the U.S. Army's Camp Upton. It served our water distribution needs for decades.
And then we demolished it!
As the tower aged, its maintenance became more difficult. So, teams from the Facilities & Operations Directorate, its Modernization Project Office, and contracting companies worked together to safely decommission this giant structure without interrupting other utility lines.
And that meant borrowing a little help from gravity.

entry.title: Researchers Demonstrate Wireless Capability for Quantum Network

media:group.media:title: Researchers Demonstrate Wireless Capability for Quantum Network
media:group.media:description:
Researchers at Brookhaven National Laboratory and Stony Brook University have successfully transmitted light particles containing quantum information through open air between the two institutions. This was the first demonstration of its kind in the United States and a key milestone toward extending the nation’s longest quantum network — already connecting eight nodes across several institutions — beyond the limits of fiber-optic cables.
During a daytime demonstration on Friday, Aug. 21, the scientists used a laser to generate quantum states of light, each containing just a few individual photons, in Stony Brook University’s state-of-the-art Quantum Watchtower. From the Watchtower, located on the roof of Stony Brook’s Health Sciences Center in Stony Brook, New York, the photons exited the core of an optical fiber only about 5 microns in diameter — less than one-tenth the width of a human hair — and traversed 13 miles (21 kilometers) to Brookhaven’s Quantum Lighthouse in Upton, New York.
Watch the replay of this live demonstration as leaders from Brookhaven and Stony Brook, as well as local, state, and federal government officials, celebrate the successful transmission.
During nighttime tests, when there are lower levels of background light, the researchers have also successfully sent entangled photons from the Stony Brook physics laboratory to the Quantum Watchtower via fiber, then distributed them across the new free-space optical link, and successfully received and measured them at the Quantum Lighthouse. This was a key advance toward achieving sustained “wireless” exchange of quantum information between the two institutions — and eventually beyond.

entry.title: The Science, Story, and Global Significance of the Electron-Ion Collider

media:group.media:title: The Science, Story, and Global Significance of the Electron-Ion Collider
media:group.media:description: Most of the mass in the visible universe originates not from atoms, but from gluons — the force-carriers that bind quarks inside protons and neutrons. Gluons also appear to play a key role in generating a fundamental quantum property of these particles: spin. Despite decades of experiments around the world, gluons remain poorly understood. The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), now under construction at Brookhaven National Laboratory, will change that. By colliding beams of electrons with protons and atomic nuclei, the EIC will produce the first detailed maps of how gluons and quarks are distributed inside matter, revealing where mass, spin, and the strong nuclear force truly come from.

media:group.media:title: Meet Newt and April 🐾
media:group.media:description:
Wildlife detection dogs Newt and April recently came to Brookhaven Lab to help locate eastern box turtles, which are a species of special concern in New York State.
By annually monitoring these turtles across several sites, researchers are building the long-term dataset needed to understand how the populations are changing and what conservation actions may help protect them.

entry.title: Student Bridges Face the Ultimate Pressure Test

media:group.media:title: Student Bridges Face the Ultimate Pressure Test
media:group.media:description: Brookhaven Lab's annual Bridge Building Competition challenges high school students across Long Island to step into the shoes of engineers. Competitors must use physics principles to design and build model bridges out of lightweight basswood. Judges place each bridge under a machine that slowly applies more pressure. Whose bridge can hold up the best in 2026?

entry.title: GridSearch: Expanding the Electric Grid with AI

media:group.media:title: GridSearch: Expanding the Electric Grid with AI
media:group.media:description:
As the demand for electricity grows, especially from facilities like data centers, researchers at Brookhaven Lab are developing AI models to expand the power grid rapidly and efficiently. GridSearch is the Lab’s “AI for AI” solution, leveraging artificial intelligence to identify optimal points where large new loads can be added to the grid. Traditional methods of simulating the electric grid can take months. GridSearch takes minutes.
Researchers at Brookhaven Lab are developing GridSearch as part of the Genesis Mission, a flagship initiative led by the U.S. Department of Energy to dramatically accelerate American scientific discovery, strengthen U.S. economic leadership, and enhance national security through AI. GridSearch supports “Securing U.S. Leadership in Data Centers” and “Scaling the Grid to Power the American Economy,” two of the Mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges.

media:group.media:title: Cloud in a Box
media:group.media:description:
These clouds aren't for gazing. ☁️
Brookhaven researchers built a convection cloud chamber that can produce clouds in a controlled environment, enabling repeatable experiments to probe the physics underlying cloud processes.

media:group.media:title: A Quantum Revolution is Approaching
media:group.media:description:
Preetha Sarkar was selected as top presenter in the Brookhaven Lab research SLAM. She will represent Brookhaven Lab at the National Lab Research Slam competition on April 15 in Washington, D.C.
The SLAM challenges early-career scientists to discuss their cutting-edge research in an easy-to-understand presentation that's only three minutes long or less.
In her winning presentation, Sarkar highlights her research on superconductors — materials that, at ultra-cold temperatures, conduct electricity without losing any energy. These materials can be used in "qubit" memory units for quantum computers.
The new qubits Sarkar is making will operate at temperatures an order of magnitude higher than the others. They will require far less complicated cooling systems, can retain information longer, and could be manufactured with techniques already used by the silicon industry.

media:group.media:title: 2025 Brookhaven Lab Research SLAM
media:group.media:description: Thirteen early career scientists worked to distill years of complex research into compelling three-minute talks for the third annual Brookhaven Lab Research SLAM.

entry.title: Final Collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider

media:group.media:title: Final Collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider
media:group.media:description:
Witness the final particle collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), where scientists have been smashing atoms since the summer of 2000.
Beams of ions — atoms stripped of their electrons — will circulate through the twin 2.4-mile-circumference RHIC rings and crash into one another at nearly the speed of light for the final time, capping off a quarter century of groundbreaking discoveries and technological advances in accelerators, detectors, and computing.
Join us in officially ending the RHIC operations era, celebrating RHIC's remarkable successes, and marking the transition of RHIC into a new state-of-the-art nuclear physics research machine, the world's first fully polarized Electron-Ion Collider.

entry.title: A VISION for an AI Lab Partner

media:group.media:title: A VISION for an AI Lab Partner
media:group.media:description: Our researchers had a VISION for an AI lab partner — and they've brought it to life. This voice-controlled assistant helps scientists interact with complex scientific instruments, streamlining experiments and accelerating discovery.

media:group.media:title: Meet sPHENIX
media:group.media:description: sPHENIX, the newest detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, is capturing snapshots of particle collisions more than three times faster than its predecessor. This enables physicists to explore the building blocks of the universe in more detail than ever before.

media:group.media:title: Embodied AI at Brookhaven Lab
media:group.media:description:
Researchers at Brookhaven Lab are making progress in many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), including “embodied AI” — systems that incorporate AI into a physical object, such as a robot, that can interact with and learn from the physical world.
Carlos Soto, from the Lab's Computing and Data Sciences Directorate, leads Brookhaven's work in embodied AI. Hear him explain this fascinating research and where it's leading.

entry.title: This radioisotope shows great promise for treating cancer

media:group.media:title: This radioisotope shows great promise for treating cancer
media:group.media:description:
Particle accelerators aren’t just for studying the universe — they're also driving breakthroughs in medicine!
Brookhaven is one of three national labs leveraging its accelerator infrastructure to produce actinium-225, a rare medical isotope that shows great promise for treating cancer.
This accelerator-produced actinium-225 will be used to treat human patients for the first time ever in a groundbreaking clinical trial beginning this year.

media:group.media:title: Superconductivity Heats Up with Nickel
media:group.media:description: Jonathan Pelliciari, a beamline scientist at Brookhaven Lab, explains how research at NSLS-II is opening a new chapter in the history of superconductivity by exploring the unique properties of nickel using cutting-edge X-ray techniques.
